What’s new.

Two lists. The first is read from GitHub as you open this page: the pull requests merged lately in the public repositories, this site’s among them, newest first. The second is each product’s own list of changes, from the statement it ships with, as of this copy, written 2026-10-20 16:23 UTC.

Merged lately

Asking GitHub for the latest merged pull requests…

    By product

    Symphony GitHub Apps

    1. Version 40 says that the Folders tab, when it opens a repository that tracks a drive already, its workflow drive-sync.yml, its drive.json on the default branch and its own secret SYMPHONY_DRIVE_REFRESH there and the connection not run out, reads the repository’s variable SYMPHONY_DRIVE and, where that is not on, sets it to on, as you, without a press of Track, so that a drive tracked before Track set the switch syncs each half hour; it writes nothing else and says on the page that it did. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed, and neither App’s permissions changed.
    2. Version 39 says that the Folders tab’s Track takes the organization’s secret only where the repository is public or the organization’s plan is a paid one, for which it reads the organization’s record and uses only its plan’s name, and only where the secret’s list of repositories reads whole, which it reads page by page; that where GitHub refuses the organization’s secret it saves the repository’s own; that it reads SYMPHONY_DRIVE_ID back after writing it; that a repository that once took the organization’s secret stays on its list; and that it sets SYMPHONY_DRIVE only where drive.json went to the default branch. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed, and neither App’s permissions changed.
    3. Version 38 says that in an organization’s repository the Folders tab’s Track saves a drive’s refresh token once for the organization, as its secret SYMPHONY_DRIVE_REFRESH, and the drive’s id as its variable SYMPHONY_DRIVE_ID, each shared with selected repositories alone, adding each repository that tracks the drive to their lists, with SymphonyBoard’s organization permissions Secrets and Variables it already held for the Tokens page, where the repository has no secret of its own, the organization’s public key is yours to read and the organization holds no such secret or one for the same drive, and otherwise the repository’s own secret as before, so another person’s drive never replaces it; that anyone who may write to any repository on the list can then reach the whole drive; and that a new connection replaces the token, and its 90-day lapse, for every repository the secret serves. It says that in a repository carrying the drive catalog’s workflow, drive-catalog.yml, and no drive sync, Track saves the secret alone, writing no drive.json and starting no run, and that workflow walks the drive from its top as the organizer’s does, with no step organize. It says that Track also sets the repository’s Actions variable SYMPHONY_DRIVE, with SymphonyBoard’s repository permission Variables it already held for the Tokens page, so that the drive sync’s schedule runs only where a drive is tracked, and that the Sync run adds the drive sync’s workflow and its scripts where an adopted repository lacks them, as it adds the Token workflow. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed, and neither App’s permissions changed.
    Earlier changes (36)
    1. Version 37 adds the environment token-store to what Symphony Setup makes in an adoption run, of either kind, as the section on the adoption says: it reads the repository’s default branch from the record it already reads, asks GitHub whether the repository has an environment of that name, through the environment’s list of deployment protection apps, which Administration reads, and where it has none makes one whose deployment branches are the default branch alone, with the Administration on the repository the Setup App already holds. It reads and writes nothing else; the environment holds no secret and no variable; the pull request says whether it was made, was there already or was not set up, quoting GitHub where it refused; and the run’s public log says only that, per setting. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed, and neither App’s permissions changed.
    2. Version 36 adds the Folders tab’s own actions on your OneDrive, as the section on the Folders tab says: new folder, rename, delete into the recycle bin, upload, download, cut, copy and paste, sharing links for viewing or editing, properties, a preview pane, a search of the whole drive and small pictures of the files in the list, each sent from your browser to Microsoft Graph alone, as you, with the access Microsoft already granted for the drive (Files.ReadWrite), and each only when you press it; what the explorer keeps it keeps in the open page’s memory alone. It says that the tab no longer reads the drive organizer’s catalog, which version 26 added, and that the drive organizer’s workflow reads the drive through Microsoft Graph alone with the repository’s drive secret and the sign-in service’s route, as drive-sync.yml does, lists without reading inside the folders Microsoft 365 keeps at the drive’s top, writes the list and texts of up to 1,500 characters from a sample of the files to the branch drive-catalog of a private repository, and, in its step organize, gives them to Claude on the repository’s own Claude token and opens issues for the projects Claude proposes. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed, and neither App’s permissions changed.
    3. Version 35 adds sign-in by code, GitHub’s device flow, built for the control panel installed as an app and switched off until the developer turns it on, as the section on the control panel says: while it is off no page offers a code; once it is on, a press of the installed app’s “Sign in with GitHub”, or in a browser’s tab of “Sign in with a code instead”, has the sign-in service’s route /device ask GitHub for a code with SymphonyBoard’s client id alone and no client secret, and the page holds the device code in the open page’s memory alone and sends it to the service’s route /device/token, at most once every five seconds, which passes it to GitHub with the client id and no client secret until you have typed the short code at https://github.com/login/device and allowed SymphonyBoard; the page then keeps what the sign-in by GitHub’s page keeps, save where the browser refuses to store the token, which a sign-in by code, needing no storage to finish, can meet: there the page holds it in its memory alone, never renews it, and “Forget the token”, or a sign-in by code or a pasted token that takes its place, drops it without asking GitHub to revoke it, so it stays good until it runs out within eight hours; and the service keeps nothing of it. It says that “Enable Device Flow”, which sign-in by code needs ticked on SymphonyBoard, lets anyone ask GitHub for a SymphonyBoard code and talk a person into typing it, which hands whoever asked a token that acts as that person, so the page warns beside every code to type only one started on that page a moment ago; and that such a sign-in’s refresh token renews at GitHub with the client id alone, each renewal good for six months more, so that it lasts until it is revoked or goes six months unrenewed, and where you revoke it; and that “Forget the token” asks GitHub to revoke each sign-in’s token that the tab’s own storage or the browser’s storage holds, and no other, so not one the browser refused to store, while whether GitHub then refuses such a sign-in’s refresh token too is not established. It names, as no earlier version did, the stylesheet of Google Fonts that the control panel and the cost page link for the site’s typefaces, Newsreader, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono, as the site’s other Symphony pages do, which your browser asks Google for, with the font files it names, as the pages load, with nothing of the page’s own in those requests, the stylesheet’s naming the page it came from by the site’s address alone and each font file’s naming the site by its origin and the stylesheet by Google’s own address alone, as browsers do unless set otherwise. And it says that the control panel installs as an app, the same page in a window of its own, whose “Sign in with GitHub” may come back from GitHub’s page to your browser rather than to the app, where the page sends the code nowhere and the code signs nobody in, while the app keeps what the press kept, as a tab does, until another press, a return or the clearing of that storage ends it, and that where the app shares its browser’s storage with that browser’s tabs it reads a sign-in or a token kept there with “Keep me signed in” ticked, and its “Forget the token” forgets that for those tabs too; earlier versions said that GitHub sends your browser back to the page, which holds in a browser’s tab alone. It also says, as no earlier version did, what a press of “Sign in with GitHub” keeps in the tab’s own storage until GitHub’s return reaches the page, or for as long as the sign-in is left unfinished: a one-time value, the sign-in’s one-time secret, whether “Keep me signed in” is ticked and the page’s query, the repository it showed. It corrects the section on the control panel’s Dependencies tab, which said that the tab writes nothing to your browser’s storage, as was so until its row of tiles came: where a repository has two charts or more, the page keeps there which of them you last chose, by the repository’s name and the chart’s, until you choose another, and neither “Forget the token” nor taking the repository off your list removes it; the list of what the page keeps in your browser now names it too. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    4. Version 34 adds the Sync run, symphony-template#257, as the section of that name says: a workflow of the developer’s in the template’s own repository that, whenever the board’s, tidy, metrics or Token workflow, scripts/tokens.py or any file under tools/ changes there, once a week and by hand, walks every installation of SymphonyBoard on the App’s own key and, in each repository an installation reaches but the template’s and the front door’s own, a fork and one archived or disabled, reads the default branch’s newest commit and the listing of its tree, and, where that branch holds docs/agents/PROTOCOL.md, the text of the switches .github/symphony-sync, .github/symphony-adopt and .github/sdlc-adopt, and, where the repository has not opted out with off in one of them, holds no .github/workflows/protocol.yml, which every copy of the whole template holds unless its owner has removed it and none adopted for the protocol alone does, so that a copy of the whole template, the front door’s or one made with “Use this template”, is passed over with nothing written while it keeps that workflow, and a file needs changing, the twenty newest pull requests from the branch symphony/sync and, unless none of the App’s among them is open and the newest of the App’s was closed unmerged offering the same files, GitHub’s comparison of the default branch with that branch, where it exists, with lines of the files changed on it, and, where every commit the branch holds beyond the default branch is the App’s own or a merge and an open pull request of the App’s offers the same files, the record of the branch’s newest commit; it writes nothing where none of the App’s pull requests among them is open and the newest of the App’s was closed unmerged offering the same files, where a commit the branch holds beyond the default branch is neither the App’s own nor a merge or the branch holds more commits beyond the default branch than GitHub’s comparison lists, or where an open pull request of the App’s offers the same files and its branch already holds one commit straight on the default branch’s newest commit; otherwise it writes the files it offers, a tree and a commit on the default branch’s newest commit as git objects in the repository, the branch symphony/sync, which it makes or moves by force, and one pull request, or a new description for the one open, writing the offer and moving the branch again on each later run that gets that far while GitHub refuses to open that pull request, as it does while one someone else opened from the branch stands open, offering the newer versions of the vendored library and of the board’s, tidy, metrics and Token workflows with their scripts, replacing only files that hold a version the template once held, adding only the Token workflow with its scripts and, to a unit the repository has by its workflow or, for the library, by tools/VENDORED, every file of that unit the repository lacks, and never offering again a pull request closed unmerged while the files it would bring, each path with the template’s version of it, are the same; it does so on an installation token with Contents, Pull requests and Workflows (write) and Metadata (read), revoked after each installation’s repositories whatever GitHub answers, and its log, which whoever may read the template reads, counts outcomes and names no repository. SymphonyBoard asks for no new permission for it: the list of what SymphonyBoard asks for now names the Sync run under Contents, Pull requests and Workflows, and the sections on keys and tokens, on what the Apps never do and on uninstalling name it too. The introduction and the section on the adoption say that only a repository that holds the claim protocol without the whole template is offered newer files, and the section on the Sync run says that a copy of the whole template made since the template holds that run carries .github/workflows/sync.yml, whose runs there skip its one job. The section on the Sync run also says, as earlier versions did not, that a branch and a pull request an App makes, the adoption’s as well as the Sync run’s, start the workflows the repository runs on a push, a new branch or a pull request, in the versions the branch holds, save one that runs on pull_request_target, which runs in the default branch’s version. From symphony-start#76, the section on the adoption says that the protocol alone brings, beside the board’s, tidy and metrics workflows, the Token workflow with the scripts it runs, tools/token_run.py and the modules of the template it imports, today tools/sealbox.py, scripts/tokens.py and tools/pool.py, held back, as that section now says in full for each workflow it brings with a script, where something of the repository’s own, a file, a link or a folder, stands where one of them goes and is not a file, or a link to a file in the repository outside its .git, that holds the template’s version byte for byte, where a file of the repository’s own, or a link of its own to anything but a folder in the repository outside its .git, stands where one of their folders goes, where the repository ignores one of them, where Python would import a file of the repository’s own in place of one of them, or where one of them stays out with another workflow that imports it too, the board’s and the metrics workflows being held back also where the vendored library will not be the template’s, and that every issue opened starts it, its jobs skipping unless the issue asks it to lend or manage a token; so the section on the control panel no longer says that a repository adopted for the claim protocol alone has no workflow Token of its own, and says that one adopted for it before the adoption brought that workflow has none until it merges a pull request the Sync run offers it, where that run offers one, and that one where a file of its own kept that workflow out has none either. And from symphony-template#257 the section on what each App asks for, and the control panel’s passage on the runs an issue starts, say that where a repository has no variable SDLC_APP_ID, which names the App beside its key, the Token workflow’s two jobs that store a token into the pool and manage one there do not run, in the Token workflow as the template holds it from this version on, and a run asked for either outside crowd mode only says so on the issue, with the repository’s own token, and closes an issue that started it, where until then those jobs started there, GitHub recording each such run as a deployment to their environment token-store, which it made in the repository the first time one ran where the repository’s plan let it have environments, and stopped at the App’s token, in a copy made before 02:26 UTC on 2026-10-19 only after the Claude sign-in, the token then held on the runner and deleted unsaved, as they still do in a copy of the whole template made before then, which keeps the Token workflow it was made with, as the section on what each App asks for now says. That passage on the runs an issue starts also says, as version 33 did not, that a run in crowd mode reads the issue’s comments, so as to say it once, and closes the issue as not planned. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    5. Version 33 adds the Notebooks tab’s Make private, the owner’s choice of 2026-10-19: where a notebook’s repository is public or internal, a button in its side panel makes it private on GitHub, as you, once you confirm, which SymphonyBoard’s repository permission Administration allows, as it allows the Share tab’s changes; the tab also reads, from the answer it already asked for, whether GitHub counts you the repository’s administrator, and offers the button only where GitHub does not say you are not. So the section on what the Apps never do no longer says that SymphonyBoard changes no setting with Administration, and the list of what SymphonyBoard asks for no longer says that it holds Administration for one thing only: Make private changes a repository’s visibility, when you press it and confirm. That section now also sets what the control panel writes as you, with SymphonyBoard’s token, apart from the writes it says the Apps never make, and says that a repository made private is not wholly yours to undo, since GitHub erases its stars and watchers and changes or removes its forks, none of which making it public again brings back. The list of what SymphonyBoard asks for, and the section on what the Apps never do, now name in full what the Share tab does with Administration (it reads the invitations waiting, invites, changes a role, removes a collaborator and withdraws an invitation), where earlier versions named only the invitation, and the section on the control panel names, as no earlier version did, the request to join that the Share tab and the Tokens page’s Add dialog open as an issue, as you, titled with your login and naming the repository, which anyone who can read the repository can read, which the Share tab lists from the repository’s open issues, and which an administrator answers there with Invite, or anyone the Share tab shows the repository’s collaborators to with a decline, each a comment on the issue and its close; the Share tab otherwise does what it did. It corrects version 32, which said that an adoption lends the person who asked a token they lent with no say: as symphony-start#72 was merged, the adoption never lends a token in the organization’s keeping, which only the organization’s owners place, counts it as none of the person’s and names it nowhere, so that where the person has no other token the run may lend, the pull request says that no token in the pool names them as its owner and the log says that no tokens were lent. The Version 32 entry below now names symphony-template#254, not #253, as the pull request that brought the Token workflow its rule for a token in the organization’s keeping, and this version says so too where it describes the Token workflow’s lends and take-backs: a lend that is not one with no say lends such a token nowhere more, and a take-back of it is refused. From symphony-template#253, it says that the Token workflow’s take-back and deletion take the two variables SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS and SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS off a repository no other of the numbered slots SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_1 to SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_32 reaches, none of them being on in every repository or in every private one, whatever the slot main, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, reaches, a take-back whether or not the token reached that repository and a deletion only where the token was on in selected repositories, reading for that which repositories each of those other slots reaches, where earlier versions said the workflow never took a repository off them; that a deletion removes the secret first and its settings after, so that one stopped partway leaves a mark on an empty slot and no longer a token marked as no one’s; and that a deletion leaves the settings and the place in SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS of another token stored in the freed slot meanwhile. Until symphony-template#253 a deletion, or the recording of an account id on a slot stored before the pool kept them, also put the repository the run was on onto the lists of repositories that may read the variables it changed, which earlier versions did not say; the workflow no longer does, so what the text says the workflow adds to those lists, the repositories a token is lent to, needed no change for it. From symphony-template#249, it says that where the repository the control panel shows has no workflow Token of its own, the page reads the organization’s repositories to find one that has it, opens the issue and starts the run there, the issue’s text naming the repository the token is for, which anyone who can read the repository the issue is on can read, even where the repository the token is for is private, and lends the token to the repository it shows, or has the run lend it there once the run has read that repository’s record and the person’s permission on it. From symphony-template#251, it says that the template’s Claude workflow starts its job for a mention of @claude only by the repository’s owner, a member of its organization or a collaborator, so for anyone else’s mention GitHub marks the job skipped and no step runs. It also corrects what earlier versions said of the Tokens page and the Token workflow. The page has no box “Add or renew a slot” to paste a Claude token into, as earlier versions said, and seals nothing in your browser: its “+ Add Token”, which earlier versions called “Add a Claude account”, has the Token workflow make the token, the page holds at most the sealed box the run posts, the slots run to SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_32, and a secret the page saves is seen by the repository it shows, not by repositories you tick; the Actions permission names the page’s buttons by the names they have, “Read use now” and “Add Token”, and the box “Your token”; and a run that makes the writes for you holds SymphonyBoard’s private key, where earlier versions said the run holds no secret. The Token workflow’s reads are now named in full: the names and records of all the organization’s Actions secrets, the public key GitHub gives for sealing them, the records of SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS and SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS with their values, the second with the login of each slot’s owner and, where it holds one, their account id, and the GitHub record of the person it acts for, and SYMPHONY_LEND_TO only for a lend with no say; a lend from the page of a token already in the pool records its lender’s account id where its settings named them by login alone; and the issue of a token in the organization’s keeping carries the word organization in place of the repositories’ ids. The records on the branch pool the page reads also hold each single model’s weekly limit and whether Claude’s answer allowed the request. And a tile’s save and its X, in an organization, add the repository the page shows to the repositories that may read the variables they write, so the login of every token’s owner, and their account id where the settings hold one, reach that repository too, which earlier versions did not say. The section on the control panel now names the Tokens page’s own reads, as you, which earlier versions did not: the names and records of the Actions secrets where the tokens live, the name and value of every Actions variable there, SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS, SYMPHONY_LEND_TO for an owner of the organization, and CLAUDE_CROWD when you press Add Token. It says that the page gives the Token workflow the public key, and the run seals the token with it and posts the sealed box, only where the page makes the writes itself, and that where the run makes them the page gives it the word pool and, for a run on another repository, the id of the repository the token is for, where earlier versions said the page always gave the key. It says that a token’s settings name its owner by login alone not only where the token was stored before the pool kept account ids but also where an owner of the organization added it or marked it as someone’s on the Tokens page, which writes a login and no account id, so that such a token too is refused from an issue and, when the person presses for it on the page, given their account id, where earlier versions named only the older tokens. And it says that a take-back posts on the issue, as a list does, the slot’s number and the ids of the repositories the token still reaches, which earlier versions did not say. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    6. Version 32 adds Symphony Setup’s two organization permissions Secrets and Variables (read and write), used only in an adoption run to add the adopted repository to the lists of repositories that read the token slots of the organization’s pool owned by the person who asked, by their login and account id, one they lent with no say among them, and, beside one of them, the pool’s two variables, as the section on what each App asks for says; it reads Symphony Setup’s installation on the organization, the settings variable, which names each slot’s owner, and the records of those secrets and of the two variables, the variables’ values among them, and no secret’s value. It says what the public log and the pull request then say, and that the lending stays whatever becomes of the pull request. It says what the run’s public log shows, now with your account id beside your login: both in the settings of the step that names the repository (your login also in the request job’s step that resolves an installation or, for a repository you named, that checks you administer it) and of every later step for a repository you named, and whether the repository belongs to an organization. It also says that the Tokens page writes the organization variable SYMPHONY_LEND_TO readable by no repository’s workflows, where version 31 said the private repositories’ workflows could read it, and closes a list an earlier page left readable by them or by every repository. It says too that a token in the organization’s keeping, one lent with no say, is placed by the organization’s owners alone, as the Token workflow has done since symphony-template#254: its lender may delete it, and no longer takes it off a repository or lends it further with an ordinary lend. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    7. Version 31 adds the control panel’s Notebooks tab, as the section on the control panel says: it reads the drive organizer’s proposal of notebooks and its catalog from the branch drive-catalog of a private repository, and whether each notebook’s repository exists and whether it is private, internal or public, and writes the proposal there, as you, when you propose, change or take out a notebook. It also names the pull request the Agents tab opens to give an agent its token slots and the files it reads for it, accounts.json and tools/pool.py, and the Tokens page’s read of the branch pool, which earlier versions left out, and says, under SymphonyBoard’s Contents permission, that the control panel writes files with it, as you, as the section on the control panel lists: the pull requests it opens, Track on the Folders tab since version 21, and now the Notebooks tab. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    8. Version 30 adds the control panel’s “Your token” box and the Token workflow’s manage job, which lists, takes back or deletes the one token in an organization’s pool whose settings name you, by your GitHub login and account id, on SymphonyBoard’s installation token; and the two kinds of issue that start the Token workflow without the page, a lend and a manage, which anyone who may open an issue on a repository carrying the workflow may use, the issue’s author being the person the run acts for and the run closing the issue; among them the lend with no say, whose token goes to the repositories the organization variable SYMPHONY_LEND_TO names, or nowhere yet, and whose lender is told the slot’s number and that the token is in the organization’s keeping. The settings variable also keeps each token’s account id beside its login and, for such a token, the word organization, which a save on the page now keeps; a token a collaborator adds is lent to the repository it was added on, and where they have a token in the pool already that one is lent and no second one is made. It says that the pool the App writes can only be the developer’s own organization’s, where the App’s key is, whose owners, the developer among them, hold the tokens lent there with each lender’s login and account id; that the Token workflow mints SymphonyBoard’s token with every permission the installation has; that the settings variable reaches every repository a token was ever lent to and is printed in runs’ logs; and that the token is held on the runner in a file until it is sealed. The developer’s collector receives nothing new.
    9. Version 29 says that Symphony Setup no longer uninstalls itself after an adoption or after a request refused because the repository is adopted already: it stays installed, acting only during an adoption run, until you uninstall it. In a repository that takes the whole template, the run also sets GitHub Actions as the only source of the check named “check” in the ruleset it created; to see GitHub Actions report that check, it reads the check runs on the branch symphony/adopt with a SymphonyBoard token limited to Checks read-only for that one repository, revoked when the settings step ends. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    10. Version 28 adds the one write SymphonyBoard makes of its own: where a collaborator who is not an owner of the organization presses “Add a Claude account”, the organization’s own Token workflow, on the App’s installation token, writes the minted slot as an organization secret and writes the organization variables SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS and SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS, so a collaborator can add a Claude slot GitHub would otherwise let only an owner add; the Claude token is sealed before it is written and the App reads and writes no other secret or variable of its own. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    11. Version 27 adds SymphonyBoard’s repository permission Variables (read and write), for the control panel’s Tokens page on a personal account’s repository, which holds a Claude slot’s settings and the list of accounts as that repository’s own Actions variables, each as you; until the permission is accepted on the App’s installation such a repository takes one Claude token, its main one. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    12. Version 26 adds the Folders tab’s read of the drive organizer’s catalog, as the section on the Folders tab says: where the repository holds the branch drive-catalog and no drive is connected, the tab reads catalog.json from that branch, with your GitHub token, and shows the folders and files it names; nothing is asked of Microsoft. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    13. Version 25 adds the Ask Claude bar’s button “Ask in claude.ai”, as the section on the control panel says: it opens claude.ai in a new tab, on your own account, with your question and what the page shows in that tab’s address; the page itself sends nothing. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    14. Version 24 adds the control panel’s Explore tab, as the section on the control panel says: a map of the repository’s work from its goals and epics down to the runs on a task’s branch, their jobs and steps and a job’s log, read as you only when you go into a level, kept in the open page’s memory and written nowhere. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    15. Version 23 adds the Folders tab’s list drawn as a file explorer, its read of each item’s path in the drive and web address, and the opening of a file from it, in its Office program on your computer or on OneDrive’s own page, which hands your browser the file’s address and nothing else. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    16. Version 22 adds the control panel’s reads of the agents’ list .github/symphony/agents.json and the agent files it names, of the repositories its “Add repository” dialog offers, and of the Share tab’s collaborators and waiting invitations, and the writes its cards and the Share tab make on your press, as you: closing an issue as not planned, closing a pull request, a pull request, from a branch of its own, that changes or deletes a worker’s file or deletes an agent’s file and its line in agents.json, and a collaborator’s or an invitation’s new role, removal or withdrawal. The page keeps nothing new. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    17. Version 21 adds the control panel’s Folders tab, as the section of that name says: a tab of the control panel’s one page, on its sign-in and the repository its bar chooses, that makes a repository of yours track files and folders of your OneDrive; the box Track asks you to tick before it tracks into a public repository, where what comes down and drive.json’s names can be read by anyone; that whoever can run a workflow on the repository can use its secret to reach your whole drive, and how to withdraw the access at Microsoft; SymphonyBoard’s repository permission Secrets (read and write), for the tab and for the Tokens page on a personal account’s repository; the tab’s reads of the repository’s drive.json, of whether its secret SYMPHONY_DRIVE_REFRESH is set and of whether it has drive-sync.yml, and of your newest repositories when you ask it to find the one you just made; Track’s three writes, as you: the secret sealed in your browser, the file drive.json, on a branch with a pull request where the default branch takes only those, and a run of drive-sync.yml; the drive’s consent at Microsoft, which returns to the control panel’s own address, and the sign-in service, which adds the client secret of the developer’s Microsoft app registration, kept on Cloudflare, answers with the drive’s access token and refresh token and keeps nothing; the tokens in the page’s memory alone, for one sitting and one GitHub account; the page’s reads of your drive’s folders through Microsoft Graph, from your browser; the refresh token passing through the service on Connect and, from the repository’s workflow, on every sync, the one exchange the service answers for any caller; and the 90 days a Microsoft refresh token lasts. It also says that the control panel talks to the sign-in service and Microsoft for the Folders tab. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    18. Version 20 adds the layout the control panel keeps in your browser: the sizes of the panels you resized and the text size you chose, numbers alone, sent nowhere. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    19. Version 19 adds the control panel’s Dependencies tab, which draws each open epic’s tasks and the issues blocking them, and the goals above their epics: the page’s reads, as you, of the sub-issues of each open issue labelled epic or goal and of the issues blocking each of an epic’s sub-issues, what GitHub’s own issue pages show, made whenever the page reads the repository’s open issues, whether or not the tab is open, at most sixty for one drawing and none once your token has fewer than a hundred calls left in its hour; and the copy of Mermaid that the developer’s site carries, which the page loads only when there is a chart to draw and which also draws the charts of the board’s STATE.md in the Board tab, only those written as the board writes them. The tab keeps what it reads in the open page alone and writes nothing, to GitHub or to your browser. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    20. Version 18 adds each token’s id and owner in its settings, the page’s read of your role in the organization, the dialog’s list of the repositories a token is on, and the token:<id> label a worker’s run puts on the issue it worked.
    21. Version 17 adds SymphonyBoard’s repository permission Administration (read and write), used only by the control panel’s Share tab to invite a collaborator you name, as you, and the Share tab’s lookup of an email address in GitHub’s user search. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    22. Version 16 adds the Tokens page’s tiles: the settings each token’s tile writes to the variable SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_SETTINGS and its label variable, and the X that deletes a slot’s secret, label, settings and place in SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_ACCOUNTS. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    23. Version 15 says that the Tokens page’s “Add a Claude account” starts the workflow Token on the repository in place of “Add with one press”, which made a Codespace: the issue it opens, the sign-in link, the code and the sealed token on that issue, the page saving the sealed box as the next slot and as CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN while that is not set, and the link to the Claude GitHub App’s install page. The page no longer makes a Codespace or saves a Codespaces secret, and the permissions Codespaces and Codespaces user secrets go unused. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    24. Version 14 adds Symphony Setup’s organization permission Administration (read and write), used only to allow “Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests” for an organization whose policy holds it off, so the sixth setting needs no step by hand there; the run reads the organization’s workflow permissions to leave the token’s default permissions as they were. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    25. Version 13 adds SymphonyBoard’s repository permission Actions (read and write), which the control panel’s buttons that start a workflow run by hand, and its reads of the runs, use as you. What the pages do is unchanged, and nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    26. Version 12 adds the Tokens page’s “Add with one press”: SymphonyBoard’s repository permission Codespaces and account permission Codespaces user secrets; the Codespace the page makes and deletes on your press; the page’s GitHub token handed to it as your Codespaces secret SYMPHONY_GITHUB_HANDOVER, seen by your own Codespaces on that repository alone and deleted once the slot is saved; the Claude token going from claude to GitHub inside the Codespace, never to the page; and the page’s reads of the organization’s secret names while it waits. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    27. Version 11 adds the control panel’s Assistant section: an issue of yours, Assistant: <your login> labelled assistant, that the page opens once per repository on your press, each question a comment of yours on it that mentions @claude and ends with a short block of the page’s state, the answer the repository’s Claude workflow writes there, reading only, the page’s reads of that issue’s comments every few seconds while it waits, its reads of whether you may write to the repository and of the assistant’s file on the default branch, and the number of that issue kept in your browser for each repository. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    28. Version 10 adds SymphonyBoard’s two organization permissions, Secrets and Variables (read and write), and the Tokens page’s “Add or renew a slot”, which seals a Claude token you paste in your browser and saves it, as you, as one of your organization’s Actions secrets, with its label and the list of slots as variables. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    29. Version 9 says where a sign-in for one tab keeps its refresh token: in the open page’s memory alone, never in the browser’s storage, so that the renewals end once that page is closed, reloaded or replaced by another page, and the sign-in then ends with its eight-hour token; that the tab’s own storage comes back with a tab the browser reopens or restores; that a pasted token is asked about at GitHub before the page keeps it; and that a sign-in’s token that a new sign-in or an accepted pasted token replaces is revoked through the service, as “Forget the token” revokes one. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    30. Version 8 adds the control panel and the cost page of the developer’s site, as the section of that name says: pages that work in your browser with a GitHub token you give them, talk to GitHub’s API as you, and, with “Sign in with GitHub”, send GitHub’s one-time code to a stateless service of the developer’s on Cloudflare that answers with the token and a refresh token and keeps nothing. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    31. Version 7 removes the sweep: no workflow on the front door lists SymphonyBoard’s installations every ten minutes and reads each repository they reach to decide whether to offer an adoption, since installing the App alone is no longer a request, the install sending you to the form, where the press is; the run reads an installation only when a form carries its number, as the adoption section now says, and the collector’s daily read of the branch metrics is as it was. With the sweep go two things the run did on its path only: it no longer reads a repository’s direct collaborators to find an administrator, since every request names the person who asked, and it no longer opens an issue in your repository when it could not open its pull request, since the form’s own issue is answered instead. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    32. Version 6 says that the run, asked for a repository with no commit yet, first makes its first commit, as GitHub’s own “Add a README file” does: a README.md holding the repository’s name, on the default branch, which Contents write allows; that it reads whether such a repository has any branch at all; that closing the pull request leaves that README; and, as it did already, that when the form carries an installation’s number the run asks of each repository both Apps reach what it asks of the one it adopts. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    33. Version 5 says that the run also reads the two switches under their names before the rename to Symphony, .github/sdlc-adopt and .github/sdlc-metrics; that an adoption never turns on a switch of the repository’s own that says off already, under either name, and brings nothing that shares where it cannot write the switch; that a repository adopted before the rename turns sharing off in .github/sdlc-metrics, the switch its workflow reads; and that Symphony Setup also uninstalls itself after a request refused because the repository is adopted already. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    34. Version 4 adds the sixth setting Symphony Setup applies: in a repository that takes the whole template, it ticks “Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests” where your organization and its enterprise allow it. It also names what the run reads to leave your settings as they are: the repository’s rulesets, its topics and its workflow permissions for GitHub Actions. Nothing the developer receives or keeps changed.
    35. Version 3 adds to METRICS.json what the work cost, as the section on field metrics describes: the tokens Claude used, by kind and by model family, their price at Anthropic’s API list prices and the date of that list, the seconds Claude was at work, the counts and rates per merge they are set against, and the comparison of work done alone with work done in parallel; and it says which records in your repository the workflow reads to make them, and that the switch stops those records too. Nothing else changed.
    36. Version 2 adds to METRICS.json and JUDGE.json the counts of how the work ran in parallel that the section on field metrics describes, and to JUDGE.json how many of its conversations had two or more people, the number of days it covered and any limit it ran under. It also says what the workflow reads to make METRICS.json, and names what the two files held already and version 1 left out: the time each was made, the number of days METRICS.json covers and the short id of the protocol’s commit, and, in JUDGE.json, how many conversations were judged, the totals of the failure types’ three groups, the model, the version of the prompt and the word that names its schema. Nothing else changed.

    1. Version 6 (extension 1.4.1) says how the popup’s links open.
    2. Version 5 (extension 1.4.0) says that the step from Symphony Setup’s install page covers its permissions page too, when it arrived without the repository.

    Beethoven

    1. Version 17 (2026-10-18, Beethoven 22.0.0): For your lab lead in Settings gains Connect GitHub Actions and Remove, which type one line each in the portal’s shell to set up or take out the grid’s ssh gate for one GitHub repository from the lab lead’s own copy of hpcworker, as the section on your cluster account says. Nothing is stored and nothing reaches Licensor. Licensor treats this change as not material to the agreement, since nothing is typed unless a lab lead presses one of the two buttons, so the agreement stays at version 15 and an acceptance of it stays in force. Version 16’s other terms are unchanged.
    2. Version 16 (2026-10-16, Beethoven 21.0.0): Settings takes the address of a project of yours on claude.ai, kept in storage.local with your other preferences until you clear it. With one given, the page Beethoven opens when a worker you started is ready, if you kept that on, and the page Open my project opens, is that project’s page in place of your session’s link, since a project takes up your worker only when you ask for the work there; New session and Copy link keep your session’s link. Beethoven makes no request to claude.ai for it and never reads the page; it notes the project’s tab it opened, as it notes your claude.ai tab, so it can bring it forward. The card that offers Settings for the address is noted with the other one-time tips. Version 15’s other terms are unchanged.
    3. Version 15 (2026-10-13, Beethoven 20.0.0): Beethoven’s listing on the Chrome Web Store is public: installing it needs no invitation, and your approval still decides whether it works. The request page no longer asks for a Google account, since no invitation is sent; a Google account given earlier stays in the access record and is no longer used. Version 14’s other terms are unchanged.
    Earlier changes (13)
    1. Version 14 (2026-10-11, drafted for Beethoven 20.0.0 and replaced by version 15 before 20.0.0 shipped): your approval works on every installation of your own: a second computer, browser profile or reinstall is approved at its first check instead of refused, Licensor’s service keeps the list of the ten most recent installations your account asked from and tells Licensor of a new one by e-mail with a link to withdraw the approval and none to move it; an installation still serves one account. Version 13’s other terms are unchanged.
    2. Version 13 (2026-10-09, Beethoven 19.0.0): Beethoven signs in to your portal for you. In Chrome, when your portal asks for a sign-in, the panel shows Beethoven’s own sign-in sheet for your account name and cluster password, and the extension answers your portal’s request for a sign-in from its background, with no tab, under the webRequest and webRequestAuthProvider permissions, which it now requests: only for its own reading of your portal’s dashboard, at most once per check, and never for a tab, a proxy, another website or another realm. It sends a password your portal turns down at most once, and that refusal stops every sign-in it makes by itself until you type the password again. Saving the password is optional and off unless you tick Remember it on this computer; a saved password is kept only encrypted, in the extension’s database in this browser profile, under a key derived from what a passkey releases (Windows Hello, Touch ID or your screen lock, named with your account name followed by “(grid)”); what the passkey releases stays in memory only, from when you unlock it until the browser closes or Beethoven updates or reloads; a password not saved is kept in memory for one sign-in and at most two minutes. New in your browser: the saved sign-in, its note, the note that a passkey could not lock a password, the unlocked secret, the typed password for one sign-in and the outcomes of the last tries (the table). Forget beside Grid sign-in in Settings, Disconnect and changing to another portal delete them. Chrome keeps a password that worked in memory until it closes and uses it for your portal tabs too. Use Chrome’s sign-in box instead keeps the way of 18.0.0, which is also the only way where the extension cannot answer a request for a sign-in. The statement now tells the old passkey of 12.0.0 to 15.0.0 apart from the new one. Nothing new reaches Licensor.
    3. Version 12 (2026-10-08, Beethoven 16.0.0): the direct way of versions 12.0.0 to 15.0.0 is removed whole. The extension no longer reaches your cluster over ssh, has no Bridge, no sign-in sheet, no key in your browser, no passkey, no Forget this computer, no phone route and no relay, holds no nativeMessaging permission, and never asks for your cluster password or verification code; it reaches your cluster only through your university’s Open OnDemand portal, behind your university’s VPN where it requires one, as versions up to 11.0.0 did. On its first run after the update it deletes from your browser what the direct way kept there, the key unread, and keeps one note where that version recorded that it had added a line to your cluster account, which Settings show once, with Forget; the Bridge on your computer, that line and a passkey are outside the browser and stay until you remove them, as the new section What an earlier version may have left says. New on your device: a press you made while the grid was out of reach waits and goes ahead by itself once the grid answers, with the extension asking your portal’s address whether it answers every three seconds while a page of Beethoven’s is open and once a minute while none is; Keep my worker running also starts a worker again that ended, at most three times in a row; and the screen that asks you to turn on your VPN links your university’s own page about it. The sections on the Bridge, the ssh sign-in, the relays and the pilot app, and on what your university sees on the ssh path, are gone with them. Nothing new reaches Licensor.
    4. Version 11 (2026-10-04, Beethoven 15.0.0): on Windows and on a Mac the Bridge is now a compiled program of Licensor’s, offered from inside the extension as a signed installer that installs into your own account without administrator rights: on Windows a Windows Installer file signed by Licensor, removed from Settings, Apps; on a Mac an installer package signed by Licensor and notarized by Apple, removed with the uninstaller beside the Bridge. On Linux the Bridge is the script it was. A Bridge installed from a zip file with an earlier version keeps working until you remove it with the uninstaller beside it. When you open a signed installer, your system may check its signature with Apple or Microsoft; that is your system’s own behaviour and tells Licensor nothing. The Bridge does what it did: it reaches only your cluster’s ssh port, carries the encrypted connection and keeps nothing. Nothing new reaches Licensor.
    5. Version 10 (2026-10-02, Beethoven 12.0.0): the extension now tries the ssh path first: an ssh connection to your cluster’s login node, with no VPN, carried by the Bridge, a small helper program that ships inside the extension and that you install once on your computer, without administrator rights; it reaches only your cluster’s ssh port and keeps nothing. The first time, you sign in on the extension’s own sign-in sheet with your account name, password and verification code, which go only to your cluster, inside the encrypted connection, and are never stored; the extension then keeps a key in your browser that no script can copy out, and adds one restricted line to your cluster account that lets that key run only a short list of commands and never sign a worker in to Claude. Protecting that key with a passkey (Windows Hello or Touch ID) is optional and off unless you turn it on. Forget this computer removes the key and the line. Where your cluster has no verification code for you, the extension shows how to set one up yourself, on a computer or on your phone, with QR codes drawn on your device. A relay is not used unless your university’s site profile names one, and this statement would name it first; the pilot app is given only to a student who asks. Without the Bridge the extension works through your portal, as before. The approval check is unchanged and is sent only after your cluster accepts your sign-in. Nothing new reaches Licensor.
    6. Version 9 (2026-10-01, Beethoven 11.0.0): the agreement is accepted on a welcome page with one box and one button, with no typed name; the acceptance record now holds the summary and the sentence shown, whether you opened, scrolled to the end of, saved or printed the full text, and, once your portal first shows it, your account name. The extension now reaches your portal from its own background, on the sign-in your browser keeps, and opens a portal tab only for you to sign in, closing it afterwards, or, on a portal that does not share its sign-in, in the background for one action; after you agree, and before you sign in, it checks whether your portal answers, with requests that carry no sign-in. One command starts your worker and, when needed, the Claude sign-in, and writes your Remote Control answer; the framework keeps a plain-words progress log for each worker. Where the portal’s shell asks for a password, a one-time step makes a key in your cluster account that only your institution’s Open OnDemand server can use; you type your password into the portal’s own terminal page, and the extension never sees it and keeps nothing about the key. New on your device: your worker’s last known state and link, how the extension reaches your portal, your last five waits, the tour and the one-time tips seen, an activity list for Show log, the tabs it opened itself, and your appearance choice; the note of the tab the toolbar button was clicked from is gone, with the activeTab permission. The QR code for your phone and the tour are drawn on your device. The statement now names what the access service keeps from the checks (how many, and the reason given with a no), the reviewers’ mock account, and that the list of approved accounts is not published, and says “no site permission on claude.ai” where it said “no access”. Nothing new reaches Licensor.
    7. Version 8 (2026-09-30, Beethoven 8.0.0): the extension no longer carries the framework’s scripts and never copies them into your account. It works only with the one shared copy your university’s lab keeps on the cluster; where there is none, or your account cannot use it, it says so and names whom to ask, and uploads nothing. The note of the install it ran no longer counts uploaded files. One approved account, one installation: the approval check now also sends the random installation identifier the extension already kept, and the service binds an approval to the first installation that asks, refuses any other until Licensor moves the approval, refuses that installation for any other account, and keeps what One approved account, one installation says. Beethoven is offered only through a private listing on the Chrome Web Store. The request page now also asks for the Google account that receives the invitation to that listing, takes an optional CV (deleted twelve months after the decision), and may ask you to confirm your university mailbox.
    8. Version 7 (2026-09-29, Beethoven 7.0.0): the product has a new name, Beethoven, and new addresses. Its pages, the support page and the request page are under https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/; the two daily files are https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/services.json and https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/killlist.json; the access service answers at https://beethoven-access.openspineconsortium.workers.dev, a second name for the same service, which keeps the same records. The request page now also tells the service which product’s page a request was sent from. Nothing about the data changed: the extension keeps, sends and receives the same items as under version 6, and Licensor records the same.
    9. Version 6 (2026-09-29, extension 5.0.0): where your institution’s lab keeps one shared, read-only copy of the cluster-side scripts, the extension no longer copies them into your account; it writes a small launcher, a one-line marker naming the lab’s copy and your profile, and reads that copy’s version file through your portal. Nothing new leaves your device and nothing new reaches Licensor. The install note the extension keeps is also written when you press “Set up the cluster again” under Details.
    10. Version 5 (2026-09-29, extension 4.0.0): there are no license keys any more, and nothing to type or paste. Your own sign-in to your portal identifies you, by the account name the portal’s dashboard shows; the extension confirms with Licensor’s access service that this account is approved when you connect, when you click the icon and about once a day, and that check is now the one request that carries anything about you (the account name, the portal’s hostname, the product and its version; Licensor records those with the time, a salted hash of the network address and the answer). The daily list withdraws versions only; the extension also reads a daily services file for the service’s address. The table rows for the key and the identifier are replaced by the account name and the last answer; the Ask for access button, which carries your account name in the page’s address, is named. Nothing else changed.
    11. Version 4 (2026-09-29): the statement now describes the software as built. Earlier versions described an activation request and optional error reports; the extension has neither (there is no code for them and no address to send them to), so the sections that described them are removed and the section “What Licensor receives” names the one request the extension makes to Licensor, the daily withdrawn-keys list. The record Licensor keeps when it issues a key is named for what it is. Nothing new leaves your device; less was ever leaving it than the earlier text said.
    12. Version 3 (2026-09-29): the extension now starts the Claude sign-in sitting for you and takes the pasted code in its own panel (the section “What happens when you sign in to Claude” is new); your statement about a worker’s workspace is kept per workspace in the browser instead of per browser session, and now includes your answer to Claude Code’s Remote Control question, which the extension records in one marker file in your cluster account; the notes the extension keeps so its automatic steps do not repeat (the last sign-in it saw, the links it opened, the check job it submitted, the install it ran) are listed; the session-state row names everything the run record holds, including the last 4,000 characters of the worker’s own log; the preference “open claude.ai when my worker connects” is added; the audit-log row says what it never holds. Nothing new leaves your device or your accounts.
    13. Version 2 (2026-09-29): added the checklist tick, the start-by-itself preference and the session’s claude.ai link to the table of what stays in your browser, and named the withdrawn-keys copy and the installation identifier that were already kept there. Nothing new leaves your device.
